LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Listen First, Think First, Speak Kindly & Solve Together — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the order that settles squabbles: not who is right, but what runs first — ears, then think, then kind words, then the together-fix.

What is this?

Listen first, think first, speak kindly and solve together are the four peace steps: full ears before any mouth, a thinking beat before speaking, kind words even in disagreement, and a fix both people can live with.

What does it mean?

Conflict is not the enemy of friendship — unhandled conflict is. Children who know the ORDER (ears, think, kind, together) turn squabbles into their first negotiations, and a four-year-old negotiator is a thing of beauty.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: listening goes FIRST because both sides need air (no interrupting — the hardest and highest skill); the think-beat is one breath between hearing and answering; and speaking kindly is not weak — it is how the strong actually win arguments.

Why this matters

This card is where the class meets real friction: two children, one toy, both certain. The feelings words set the table; this card serves the meal — the actual mechanics of two people finding the together-fix.

What it teaches

Conflict resolution sequencing, active listening under disagreement, prosocial assertion (kind AND firm), and joint problem-solving — the together-fix as the earliest form of compromise.

Words to learn

listen firstthink firstspeak kindlysolve togetherboth sidesfixfair

Say this to your child

“"Squabbles have an order, and here it is. Listen first — ALL the way to the end of what they are saying; ears open, mouth shut, even when you already know you are right (especially then). Think first — one breath between their words and yours: what did they actually mean? Speak kindly — you can be firm AND kind at the same time; roars make ears close, kind words keep them open. Solve together — not I-win, not you-win: the fix BOTH of us can live with. Two bears, one honey pot? Listen, think, speak kindly… and split it, or take turns, or find a bear who already ate. The order does the work."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The four steps that settle any squabble."
  2. Read the panels: the ear-hand girl LISTENs FIRST, the chin-thinking boy THINKs FIRST, the open-hand boy SPEAKs KINDLY, the two facing children SOLVE TOGETHER.
  3. Drill the order with a prop squabble: two bears, one honey pot. You narrate each step as the bears run it — ears (each bear says what it heard the other say), think (one breath), kind (no roars), together (both bears’ fix).
  4. Deploy it on the next real dispute as the narrator: you speak the step-names, the children do the steps.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "the fix is never me-win — it is us-fixed."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels run the peace process: Listen First, a girl listening with a hand to her ear; Think First, a boy pondering with a finger to his chin; Speak Kindly, a boy talking with an open friendly hand; and Solve Together, two children talking face to face — the order drawn exactly as it should be run.

Ask your child

"What comes before the mouth?" "How long is the think-first beat?" "Can you be firm and kind at the same time?" "Whose fix is it in the end?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Ears first!" "Let me think for a second" (the beat, arriving) or the negotiated one: "we could take turns AND share the top."

Out in the real world

Disputes queue up daily: the swing, the front seat, the last sticker, the loudest singer. Run the order as narrator on the small ones — naming each step as it happens — and by the umpteenth small one, the children run the steps without you. Then retire gracefully to the refreshments.

Try it together

The Bear Court: a squabble is brought before the family’s wisest bear (a teddy on a cushion). The bear (voiced by your child, ideally) enforces the order: each side speaks, the OTHER side must say back what it heard, one think-breath, kind words only, then the together-fix proposed by the cubs themselves. Bear adjourns with a gavel paw. Silly, sacred, and it teaches the sequence better than any diagram.

Understanding check

Ask: "What runs first? What sits between hearing and answering? Whose fix wins?" Ears, one breath, both of us — three answers and the peace process is in service.

Parent tips

Narrate the steps, not the verdict: "that was listen-first… now the think-breath…" — children doing the steps need the step-names, not a judge. And when the together-fix is lopsided (always give the little one the honey), let it stand: fairness calibrates over months of practice, and a fix both AGREED to is the lesson, whatever the honey math.

This lesson pairs with the Listen First, Think First, Speak Kindly & Solve Together flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
